title: Microsoft's First-Quarter Results to Match Views Amid Azure's Momentum, Morgan Stanley Says
detail:
PREMIUM
Microsoft's First-Quarter Results to Match Views Amid Azure's Momentum, Morgan Stanley Says
MT Newswires

MSFT
Trade MSFT on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
microsoft -Shutterstock

Microsoft's (MSFT) fiscal first-quarter results will likely meet Wall Street's expectations, driven by sustained momentum in its Azure cloud computing platform, Morgan Stanley said Monday.

Morgan Stanley projects earnings of $4.73 per share for Microsoft, matching the consensus and surging from $3.72 a year earlier. The brokerage expects revenue of $90.24 billion, compared with the Street's estimate of a nearly 17% growth to $90.64 billion.

The technology giant is scheduled to release its quarterly results on Oct. 28.

The buyside expects 47% revenue growth for Azure in constant currency terms, which Morgan Stanley said exceeds management's 44% to 45% guidance. This estimate, coupled with a second-quarter outlook indicating at least steady year-over-year growth versus the first quarter performance, should underpin the stock price, according to the research note.

"The narrative around Microsoft has materially improved following last quarter's better results and initial (fiscal 2027) guidance pointing to durable strength across the company's core growth businesses," Morgan Stanley said. "On Azure, demand remains robust across both core cloud and (artificial intelligence) workloads."

Microsoft said in July that fiscal fourth-quarter intelligent cloud revenue soared 32% year over year, buoyed by a 43% jump in Azure and other services.

Amazon.com (AMZN) and Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL) also reported sharp cloud gains for the second quarter, with sales at the Amazon Web Services marking the fastest rate in 18 quarters. The Google cloud segment soared 82%.

The brokerage said that Microsoft continued to be the biggest winner from heavy spending on AI-related products and services.

"Importantly, we see greater data center capacity availability providing an additional tailwind to Azure growth, with our latest capacity tracker estimating that Microsoft brought (about 3.25 gigawatt) of incremental capacity online in (fiscal 2026), while we expect another (roughly) 4.25 GW to come online in (fiscal 2027)," the firm said.

Morgan Stanley also sees strong gains from Microsoft 365, the company's subscription-based service, helping it sustain the momentum into the first quarter.

"Within M365, our latest partner checks point to continued strength in E3-to-E5 upgrades, with security remaining a key driver, while early E7 adoption provides another lever for potential (average revenue per user) upside, and Copilot adoption continues to improve, although consumption-based Copilot usage remains early days," the firm said.

Microsoft's shares were up 1.1% in late afternoon trade, taking the stock's year-to-date gains to nearly 11%.

title: Want to live off dividends in retirement? Here’s how much you’d need to invest — and 5 strategies to generate income

Dividend investing has long been a popular strategy for Americans hoping to generate enough passive income to cover their living expenses. After all, who wouldn't want their investments to pay them regularly without having to sell shares?

But building a portfolio that produces meaningful dividend income has become more challenging, especially if you're relying on traditional index funds.

Consider the S&P 500. At the end of 1981, the index offered a dividend yield of 5.36%, according to Multpl (1). As of October 2026, that yield has fallen to approximately 1.04%.

Part of the reason is that some of the market's biggest companies pay relatively small dividends. Tech giants such as Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) and Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) have delivered substantial growth for investors, but their dividend yields remain comparatively low.

Even the so-called dividend aristocrats — companies that have increased their dividends for at least 25 consecutive years — aren't necessarily the answer. Some offer attractive yields, but others pay considerably less. Morningstar identified Clorox as one of the higher-yielding aristocrats earlier this year, with a forward dividend yield of 5.51% as of May 29 (2).

So, how much money would you actually need invested to live off dividends in 2026?

The answer depends on how much income you need and the investments you choose. And while dividend-paying stocks can be part of the solution, there are other ways to generate income from your savings.

Here's what to consider.

How much do you need invested to live off dividends?

The amount you need depends largely on the yield your investments generate.

For example, if you want $40,000 in annual dividend income, here's how much you would need invested at different hypothetical yields:

3% yield: Approximately $1.33 million

4% yield: $1 million

5% yield: $800,000

6% yield: Approximately $667,000

That means a portfolio generating a 5% annual yield could theoretically provide $40,000 in income with $800,000 invested.

title: Should You Buy This Trump AI Stock Ahead of Earnings?
detail:
Should You Buy This Trump AI Stock Ahead of Earnings?
Fahad Saleem
Mon, October 19, 2026 at 12:11 PM CDT 4 min read
MSFT
OPAI.PVT
Trade MSFT on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) reports quarterly results on Oct 28, and the stock ranks eighth in our list of the 10 stocks in Trump's latest stock portfolio. Click to see the other nine. Trump bought Microsoft five times in August.

Bull Case

Bulls see Microsoft as the AI company with the most ways to get paid. Customers rent its Azure cloud to run AI, and they also buy AI tools built into the software they already use, like Copilot. Demand for Azure is higher than the computing power Microsoft can supply, and management said the new capacity it added in the June quarter was used almost right away. Azure growth reached 43% that quarter, and management expects it to speed up to about 45% in the current quarter. Growth in the backlog of signed cloud work came mostly from customers outside OpenAI, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call. Big investors back the story. Ken Fisher's Fisher Asset Management raised its Microsoft stake by 3% in the second quarter, and Microsoft ranks fourth in our list of his 10 best AI stocks. Click to see the other nine picks.

Bear Case

Bears point to the bill. Microsoft's capital spending keeps rising, and Deutsche Bank analysts have warned that free cash flow could fall close to breakeven in fiscal 2027. About two-thirds of the spending goes to chips and other short-lived equipment, CFO Amy Hood said on the July earnings call. Chip and memory prices have also jumped. Some investors see a hedge. Wedgewood Partners thinks gains on Microsoft's OpenAI stake could offset higher chip and memory costs from the buildout. Check the full letter here. OpenAI is also a concentration risk. It made up about 45% of Microsoft's commercial backlog in the December quarter, so a slowdown at OpenAI would hit the backlog too. The software side faces a threat as well, because AI coding tools and rival assistants compete with Copilot and could pressure per-seat pricing. Hedge funds are trimming even a stock they love. Microsoft ranks second in our list of the 40 most popular stocks among hedge funds, and the number of hedge funds holding it fell from 282 to 273 in the second quarter, according to Insider Monkey's database. Click to see the other 39.

Ken Wolter / Shutterstock.com

Valuation

Microsoft trades at 26.75 times forward earnings, a 27% premium to the sector median of 21.01. It is also 12% below its own five-year average of 30.47. On a GAAP basis the forward P/E is 26.83, below the sector median of 28.10. The premium comes with growth. Analysts expect earnings per share to grow about 20% and revenue about 18%. Pairing the P/E with that growth gives a PEG ratio of 1.70 against a sector median of 1.14, and it sits 25% below Microsoft's own five-year average of 2.27. Investors pay more than for the average tech stock, and less than they usually pay for Microsoft.

Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT) and Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN) run the two biggest public clouds, and both clouds grew faster last quarter. Azure grew 43% in Microsoft's fiscal fourth quarter. AWS grew 37%, its fastest pace in 18 quarters. Both report their September quarters soon, and Wall Street wants proof that record AI spending is still turning into revenue.

gorodenkoff / Getty Images
Copilot Drives Azure While Custom Chips Drive AWS

Microsoft's growth came from software built on top of its own infrastructure. Microsoft 365 Copilot has passed 30 million paid seats. GitHub Copilot revenue grew over 60% quarter-over-quarter after Microsoft switched it to usage-based billing. That switch matters because customers now pay for how much they use, on top of a flat seat fee. Chief financial officer Amy Hood said efficiency gains get "quickly monetized in quarter" because demand still exceeds supply.

Amazon's story was about chips. Its AI and chips businesses each passed $25 billion annualized run rates. 98% of its top 1,000 EC2 customers use its Graviton processors. Chief executive Andy Jassy sees "a real chance" that Amazon will sell its Trainium AI chips to data centers outside its own cloud. Retail helps too: advertising revenue rose 26%, giving Amazon a high-margin stream that offsets some of its heavy spending.
